studies.title: Heightened aversion to risk and loss in depressed patients with a suicide attempt history.
studies.abstract: Suicide attempters have been found to be impaired in decision-making; however, their specific biases in evaluating uncertain outcomes remain unclear. Here we tested the hypothesis that suicidal behavior is associated with heightened aversion to risk and loss, which might produce negative predictions about uncertain future events. Forty-five depressed patients with a suicide attempt history, 47 nonsuicidal depressed patients, and 75 healthy controls participated in monetary decision-making tasks assessing risk and loss aversion. Suicide attempters compared with the other groups exhibited greater aversion to both risk and loss during gambles involving potential loss. Risk and loss aversion correlated with each other in the depressed patients, suggesting that a common pathophysiological mechanism underlies these biases. In addition, emotion regulation via suppression, a detrimental emotional control strategy, was positively correlated with loss aversion in the depressed patients, also implicating impairment in regulatory processes. A preliminary fMRI study also found disrupted neural responses to potential gains and losses in the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex, insula cortex, and left amygdala, brain regions involved in valuation, emotion reactivity, and emotion regulation. The findings thus implicate heightened negative valuation in decision-making under risk, and impaired emotion regulation in depressed patients with a history of suicide attempts.

studies.title: Smoothness without smoothing: why Gaussian naive Bayes is not naive for multi-subject searchlight studies.
studies.abstract: Spatial smoothness is helpful when averaging fMRI signals across multiple subjects, as it allows different subjects' corresponding brain areas to be pooled together even if they are slightly misaligned. However, smoothing is usually not applied when performing multivoxel pattern-based analyses (MVPA), as it runs the risk of blurring away the information that fine-grained spatial patterns contain. It would therefore be desirable, if possible, to carry out pattern-based analyses which take unsmoothed data as their input but which produce smooth images as output. We show here that the Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB) classifier does precisely this, when it is used in "searchlight" pattern-based analyses. We explain why this occurs, and illustrate the effect in real fMRI data. Moreover, we show that analyses using GNBs produce results at the multi-subject level which are statistically robust, neurally plausible, and which replicate across two independent data sets. By contrast, SVM classifiers applied to the same data do not generate a replication, even if the SVM-derived searchlight maps have smoothing applied to them. An additional advantage of GNB classifiers for searchlight analyses is that they are orders of magnitude faster to compute than more complex alternatives such as SVMs. Collectively, these results suggest that Gaussian Naive Bayes classifiers may be a highly non-naive choice for multi-subject pattern-based fMRI studies.

studies.title: Distributed neural representation of expected value.
studies.abstract: Anticipated reward magnitude and probability comprise dual components of expected value (EV), a cornerstone of economic and psychological theory. However, the neural mechanisms that compute EV have not been characterized. Using event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined neural activation as subjects anticipated monetary gains and losses that varied in magnitude and probability. Group analyses indicated that, although the subcortical nucleus accumbens (NAcc) activated proportional to anticipated gain magnitude, the cortical mesial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) additionally activated according to anticipated gain probability. Individual difference analyses indicated that, although NAcc activation correlated with self-reported positive arousal, MPFC activation correlated with probability estimates. These findings suggest that mesolimbic brain regions support the computation of EV in an ascending and distributed manner: whereas subcortical regions represent an affective component, cortical regions also represent a probabilistic component, and, furthermore, may integrate the two.

studies.title: Error monitoring using external feedback: specific roles of the habenular complex, the reward system, and the cingulate motor area revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging.
studies.abstract: The dopaminergic system has been shown to be involved in the processing of rewarding stimuli, specifically of errors in reward prediction, in animal studies as well as in recent neuroimaging studies in humans. Furthermore, a specific role of dopamine in the human homolog of the rostral cingulate motor area (rCMA) was proposed in a recent model of error detection. Negative feedback as well as self-detected errors elicit a negative event-related brain potential probably generated in the rCMA. We performed two experiments using functional magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the brain activity related to negative and positive feedback in a dynamically adaptive motion prediction task. Whereas positive feedback raised hemodynamic activity in the ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens), negative feedback activated the rCMA, the inferior anterior insula, and the epithalamus (habenular complex). These data demonstrate the role of the habenular complex in the control of the human reward system, a function previously hypothesized on the basis of animal research. The rCMA reacted only to errors with negative feedback but not to errors without feedback, which ruled out an influence of response conflict or uncertainty on its role in error detection by external signals.

studies.title: Post-conventional moral reasoning is associated with increased ventral striatal activity at rest and during task.
studies.abstract: People vary considerably in moral reasoning. According to Kohlberg's theory, individuals who reach the highest level of post-conventional moral reasoning judge moral issues based on deeper principles and shared ideals rather than self-interest or adherence to laws and rules. Recent research has suggested the involvement of the brain's frontostriatal reward system in moral judgments and prosocial behaviors. However, it remains unknown whether moral reasoning level is associated with differences in reward system function. Here, we combined arterial spin labeling perfusion and blood oxygen level-dependent functional magnetic resonance imaging and measured frontostriatal reward system activity both at rest and during a sequential risky decision making task in a sample of 64 participants at different levels of moral reasoning. Compared to individuals at the pre-conventional and conventional level of moral reasoning, post-conventional individuals showed increased resting cerebral blood flow in the ventral striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Cerebral blood flow in these brain regions correlated with the degree of post-conventional thinking across groups. Post-conventional individuals also showed greater task-induced activation in the ventral striatum during risky decision making. These findings suggest that high-level post-conventional moral reasoning is associated with increased activity in the brain's frontostriatal system, regardless of task-dependent or task-independent states.

studies.title: The Neural Correlates of Hierarchical Predictions for Perceptual Decisions.
studies.abstract: Sensory information is inherently noisy, sparse, and ambiguous. In contrast, visual experience is usually clear, detailed, and stable. Bayesian theories of perception resolve this discrepancy by assuming that prior knowledge about the causes underlying sensory stimulation actively shapes perceptual decisions. The CNS is believed to entertain a generative model aligned to dynamic changes in the hierarchical states of our volatile sensory environment. Here, we used model-based fMRI to study the neural correlates of the dynamic updating of hierarchically structured predictions in male and female human observers. We devised a crossmodal associative learning task with covertly interspersed ambiguous trials in which participants engaged in hierarchical learning based on changing contingencies between auditory cues and visual targets. By inverting a Bayesian model of perceptual inference, we estimated individual hierarchical predictions, which significantly biased perceptual decisions under ambiguity. Although "high-level" predictions about the cue-target contingency correlated with activity in supramodal regions such as orbitofrontal cortex and hippocampus, dynamic "low-level" predictions about the conditional target probabilities were associated with activity in retinotopic visual cortex. Our results suggest that our CNS updates distinct representations of hierarchical predictions that continuously affect perceptual decisions in a dynamically changing environment.

studies.title: The influence of contextual reward statistics on risk preference.
studies.abstract: Decision theories mandate that organisms should adjust their behaviour in the light of the contextual reward statistics. We tested this notion using a gambling choice task involving distinct contexts with different reward distributions. The best fitting model of subjects' behaviour indicated that the subjective values of options depended on several factors, including a baseline gambling propensity, a gambling preference dependent on reward amount, and a contextual reward adaptation factor. Combining this behavioural model with simultaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging we probed neural responses in three key regions linked to reward and value, namely ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra (VTA/SN), ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and ventral striatum (VST). We show that activity in the VTA/SN reflected contextual reward statistics to the extent that context affected behaviour, activity in the vmPFC represented a value difference between chosen and unchosen options while VST responses reflected a non-linear mapping between the actual objective rewards and their subjective value. The findings highlight a multifaceted basis for choice behaviour with distinct mappings between components of this behaviour and value sensitive brain regions.

studies.title: Sleep sharpens sensory stimulus coding in human visual cortex after fear conditioning.
studies.abstract: Efficient perceptual identification of emotionally-relevant stimuli requires optimized neural coding. Because sleep contributes to neural plasticity mechanisms, we asked whether the perceptual representation of emotionally-relevant stimuli within sensory cortices is modified after a period of sleep. We show combined effects of sleep and aversive conditioning on subsequent discrimination of face identity information, with parallel plasticity in the amygdala and visual cortex. After one night of sleep (but neither immediately nor after an equal waking interval), a fear-conditioned face was better detected when morphed with another identity. This behavioral change was accompanied by increased selectivity of the amygdala and face-responsive fusiform regions. Overnight neural changes can thus sharpen the representation of threat-related stimuli in cortical sensory areas, in order to improve detection in impoverished or ambiguous situations. These findings reveal an important role of sleep in shaping cortical selectivity to emotionally-relevant cues and thus promoting adaptive responses to new dangers.

studies.title: Dissociable systems for gain- and loss-related value predictions and errors of prediction in the human brain.
studies.abstract: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons projecting to the ventral striatum code for reward magnitude and probability during reward anticipation and then indicate the difference between actual and predicted outcome. It has been questioned whether such a common system for the prediction and evaluation of reward exists in humans. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging and a guessing task in two large cohorts, we are able to confirm ventral striatal responses coding both reward probability and magnitude during anticipation, permitting the local computation of expected value (EV). However, the ventral striatum only represented the gain-related part of EV (EV+). At reward delivery, the same area shows a reward probability and magnitude-dependent prediction error signal, best modeled as the difference between actual outcome and EV+. In contrast, loss-related expected value (EV-) and the associated prediction error was represented in the amygdala. Thus, the ventral striatum and the amygdala distinctively process the value of a prediction and subsequently compute a prediction error for gains and losses, respectively. Therefore, a homeostatic balance of both systems might be important for generating adequate expectations under uncertainty. Prevalence of either part might render expectations more positive or negative, which could contribute to the pathophysiology of mood disorders like major depression.

studies.title: Dopamine agonists diminish value sensitivity of the orbitofrontal cortex: a trigger for pathological gambling in Parkinson's disease?
studies.abstract: The neurobehavioral underpinnings of pathological gambling are not well understood. Insight might be gained by understanding pharmacological effects on the reward system in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). Treatment with dopamine agonists (DAs) has been associated with pathological gambling in PD patients. However, how DAs are involved in the development of this form of addiction is unknown. We tested the hypothesis that tonic stimulation of dopamine receptors specifically desensitizes the dopaminergic reward system by preventing decreases in dopaminergic transmission that occurs with negative feedback. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, we studied PD patients during three sessions of a probabilistic reward task in random order: off medication, after levodopa (LD) treatment, and after an equivalent dose of DA (pramipexole). For each trial, a reward prediction error value was computed using outcome, stake, and probability. Pramipexole specifically changed activity of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) in two ways that were both associated with increased risk taking in an out-of-magnet task. Outcome-induced activations were generally higher with pramipexole compared with LD or off medication. In addition, only pramipexole greatly diminished trial-by-trial correlation with reward prediction error values. Further analysis yielded that this resulted mainly from impaired deactivation in trials with negative errors in reward prediction. We propose that DAs prevent pauses in dopamine transmission and thereby impair the negative reinforcing effect of losing. Our findings raise the question of whether pathological gambling may in part stem from an impaired capacity of the OFC to guide behavior when facing negative consequences.

studies.title: Interference control during recognition of facial affect enhances the processing of expression specific properties--an event-related fMRI study.
studies.abstract: Though we can almost pre-attentively categorize the valence of facial expressions, we experience emotional ambiguity when confronted with facial expressions in a context with incongruent emotional information. We simultaneously presented interfering background colors during forced-choice categorizations of negative (fear), neutral and positive (happy) expressions. Conflicting information induced strong and differential interference effects on a behavioral level which was mirrored in comparable activations on a neuronal level. Besides a common fronto-parietal attention network which was activated during interference resolution, we found differential interference effects for facial expressions. Incongruent trials with neutral expressions induced a distinct activation pattern in ventral visual regions particularly involved in deeper analysis for both the task-relevant facial expressions (fusiform (FFA) and occipital face area (OFA)) and the task-irrelevant color (V4). Compared to neutral expressions, incongruent trials including either negative or positive expressions elicited attenuated interference effects. Unlike incongruent trials with positive facial expressions which showed only sparse activation in frontal cortex, interference resolution during processing of negative facial expressions resulted in specific activations in regions (V3a, MT(+), STS) which might be involved in processing of implicit dynamics of negative expressions. Thus, functional activations in visual processing regions might specifically be related to processing demands of different expressions.

studies.title: Sex-Steroid Hormone Manipulation Reduces Brain Response to Reward.
studies.abstract: Mood disorders are twice as frequent in women than in men. Risk mechanisms for major depression include adverse responses to acute changes in sex-steroid hormone levels, eg, postpartum in women. Such adverse responses may involve an altered processing of rewards. Here, we examine how women's vulnerability for mood disorders is linked to sex-steroid dynamics by investigating the effects of a pharmacologically induced fluctuation in ovarian sex steroids on the brain response to monetary rewards. In a double-blinded placebo controlled study, healthy women were randomized to receive either placebo or the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist (GnRHa) goserelin, which causes a net decrease in sex-steroid levels. Fifty-eight women performed a gambling task while undergoing functional MRI at baseline, during the mid-follicular phase, and again following the intervention. The gambling task enabled us to map regional brain activity related to the magnitude of risk during choice and to monetary reward. The GnRHa intervention caused a net reduction in ovarian sex steroids (estradiol and testosterone) and increased depression symptoms. Compared with placebo, GnRHa reduced amygdala's reactivity to high monetary rewards. There was a positive association between the individual changes in testosterone and changes in bilateral insula response to monetary rewards. Our data provide evidence for the involvement of sex-steroid hormones in reward processing. A blunted amygdala response to rewarding stimuli following a rapid decline in sex-steroid hormones may reflect a reduced engagement in positive experiences. Abnormal reward processing may constitute a neurobiological mechanism by which sex-steroid fluctuations provoke mood disorders in susceptible women.

abstract_screening_results.reason: Meets inclusion criteria: English empirical fMRI study with original data; participants performed the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (risky decision-making); sample includes schizophrenia patients and healthy controls. No exclusion criteria met (not PET/review).

Abstract describes an English-language empirical study with original data using fMRI while human participants performed a decision-making task involving risk and effort, meeting inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria are met from the abstract. Include for full-text review.

The study uses fMRI to investigate motor sequence learning, not risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making. Inclusion met: I1 (English empirical study), I3 (human participants). Inclusion not met: I2 (fMRI during risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making). No exclusion criteria clearly met.

Empirical human fMRI study using a gambling (risky decision-making) task; original data reported. Meets inclusion: I1 (English empirical), I2 (fMRI during risky decision-making), and I3 (human participants). No exclusion criteria met (not PET or review). Include for full-text review to confirm participant details and task specifics.

Empirical fMRI study in English with original data (I1). Functional MRI was performed while participants completed the CUPS mixed-gamble task (risky decision-making) satisfying I2. Human sample includes casual methamphetamine users and non-users (I3). No exclusion criteria met (no non-fMRI-only methods, not a review). Abstract clearly matches the meta-analysis objective of fMRI studies of risky decision-making.

English-language empirical study reporting original human fMRI data where participants performed a perceptual decision-making task (judging average color/shape). Meets I1, I2, and I3 (human observers—healthy participants implied). No exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) apply based on the abstract. Include for full-text review.

fMRI was conducted on human participants during a simulated slot machine task, meeting I1 (original human study) and I3 (human participants). The abstract does not clearly state whether participants performed a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task (I2 uncertain). Because I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone, include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

EXCLUDED because the study used resting-state fMRI rather than an fMRI scan conducted while participants performed a risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making task (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (English empirical study with original data), I3 (human healthy sample). Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not demonstrated: I2 (task-based fMRI during decision-making).

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study in human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task with concurrent metacognitive reports; no exclusion criteria (e.g., PET-only or review) are met. Recommend full-text review.

English-language empirical fMRI study with original data. Participants performed a treatment probability-discounting task (risky decision-making) during fMRI and sample consisted of healthy human participants. No exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) are met.

This is an English-language empirical fMRI study reporting original data on perceptual decision-making of affective voices in human participants, meeting the review focus. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET or a review). Abstract gives sufficient information to include for full-text review.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical study with original data using model-based fMRI while human participants performed a temporally extended categorization task (perceptual decision-making). This meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria are met from the abstract. Include for full-text review to extract details.

Human 7T-fMRI empirical study (NeuroImage) where participants performed a task involving probabilistic, ambiguous, and incongruent visual sequences requiring expectancy/decision under uncertainty — fits risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making. Original data reported; no exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) apply.

Study used human EEG (scalp recordings) with source reconstruction, not functional MRI. Exclusion E1 applies. Inclusion I1 (English empirical with original data) and I3 (human participants) are met; I2 (fMRI scan during decision-making task) is not met or demonstrated.

Abstract reports original empirical data comparing adolescents with ADHD and OCD during decision making under ambiguity, meeting I1 and I3. The abstract does not explicitly state that functional MRI was used during task performance (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to confirm fMRI methods.

fMRI study with original human data assessing neural response to uncertain reward. Inclusion: I1 (original English empirical study) and I3 (human adult sample) are met. It is unclear from the abstract whether the reward task involved risky/ambiguous decision-making (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria (E1, E2) are met. Include for full-text review to confirm whether the task meets the review's decision-making requirement.

Abstract reports an empirical fMRI study (olfactory decision-making) confirming model predictions in cortical areas; implies human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task. Meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, I3. No exclusion criteria met (not PET-only, not a review). Recommend inclusion for full-text review to confirm participant details and analyses.

Study reports original human data in English, used fMRI during a risky decision-making task (BART) in healthy participants; exclusion criteria not met. Full text review warranted to extract coordinates and details.

EXCLUDE: The study used an associative taste reward (temporal difference) fMRI task examining EV/PE for food stimuli, not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (English empirical study with original data), I3 (human clinical and healthy participants). Inclusion criterion not met: I2 (fMRI task is reward learning/taste, not risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making). No exclusion criteria (E1/E2) were met.

Abstract describes an original English-language empirical human study reporting neural (striatal) activation linked to perceptual decision making urgency, indicating fMRI during task and involving human participants (likely healthy). No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET-only or review) are met. Include for full-text review.

Abstract reports an original experimental study in English with human participants performing risky monetary choices while undergoing model-based fMRI; meets I1, I2, and I3 and no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study using the Cambridge Gambling Task (risky decision-making) in healthy human participants. Meets I1 (original empirical study), I2 (fMRI during a decision-making task), and I3 (healthy human sample). No exclusion criteria apply (not PET/other non-fMRI and not a review). Include for full-text review.

E1 met: study used EEG with fMRI-informed source imaging but did not report conducting fMRI scans during the decision-making task. Inclusion met: I1 (English empirical original data) and I3 (human participants). Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (no evidence that a functional MRI scan was conducted while participants performed the perceptual decision task).

Abstract reports original empirical fMRI data (English) using a two-choice probabilistic monetary ‘wheel of fortune’ decision-making task in healthy adult humans, meeting I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (e.g., non-fMRI or review) are met. Recommend full-text review for data extraction.

Abstract describes an empirical study of OCD and decision-making/learning with fronto-striatal dysfunction but does not explicitly state that fMRI was conducted during a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task. I1 and I3 appear met; I2 is not demonstrated in the abstract. Include for full-text review to confirm fMRI task details.

Empirical human perceptual decision-making study reporting brain activation during a face/house detection task (I1 and I3 met). Abstract implies neuroimaging but does not explicitly state fMRI, so I2 is uncertain — include for full-text review to confirm fMRI acquisition.

Abstract reports an fMRI study with original data (Iowa Gambling Task) assessing ambiguous decision-making in newly diagnosed T2DM patients and controls, meeting I1 and I2. It is unclear whether the clinical population (T2DM) fits the review’s specified participant groups (I3 not clearly met), and no exclusion criteria apply. Include for full-text review to confirm participant eligibility and extract coordinates/results.

fMRI was used with human subjects during a sequential prediction/pattern-learning task, but the abstract does not explicitly state the task is a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task. Inclusion is uncertain from abstract alone, so include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Meets inclusion criteria: English empirical study (PNAS) with original data; fMRI acquired during a reward-processing task linked to decision-making and adult risk-taking; human sample (followed from childhood to young adulthood). No exclusion criteria (no PET/review). Include for full-text review to confirm task fits risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making definitions.

Abstract reports an original empirical fMRI study in humans performing a perceptual decision-making task (degraded face/house stimuli). This directly matches the review objective (perceptual decision-making) and meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET-only or review) are met based on the abstract.

Abstract reports two empirical fMRI experiments in human participants performing prediction/decision tasks with manipulated uncertainty (probability and rule knowledge). It is in English and presents original data; it directly addresses decision-making under risk/ambiguity/perceptual uncertainty. No exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) are met.

Excluded because inclusion criterion I2 is not met: the fMRI task was an intertemporal delay-discounting task (immediate vs. future rewards), which does not clearly fall under risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making as specified by the review objective. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (English empirical study) and I3 (human adolescent substance users). No exclusion criteria (E1, E2) are met.

Human fMRI study examining auditory and tactile perceptual decision-making; the abstract indicates original empirical data in English and human participants. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract describes an original, English-language empirical study using fMRI while human participants performed a risky economic decision-making task (safe vs gamble), engaging conditioned stimuli—meeting I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (E1, E2) apply from abstract information.

Empirical human fMRI study where participants underwent multisession fMRI while learning temporal sequences and making predictions (selecting most probable outcomes vs matching), which constitutes perceptual decision-making. Participants are human (male and female). No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET or review) are met. Abstract provides sufficient evidence that I1, I2, and I3 are satisfied.

Empirical human fMRI study involving substance-using young adults (I1, I3 satisfied). Abstract indicates BOLD signals but does not state that fMRI was conducted during a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to determine whether I2 (decision-making task) is met.

Empirical fMRI study in humans performing multiple perceptual decision-making tasks, reporting BOLD responses and network interactions. Meets I1 (original English study), I2 (fMRI during perceptual decision-making), and I3 (human participants). No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review.

Human fMRI study with original data where adults learned auditory/visual probabilistic sequences and reported confidence (meets I1,I2,I3). Abstract does not explicitly label the task as risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making, but it involves perceptual (auditory/visual) probabilistic inference and confidence judgments; uncertainty about fit to review objective remains, so include for full-text review to confirm.

Human fMRI study of decision-making with original empirical data addressing ambiguity in intertemporal choices (time-ambiguity). Fits review topic (ambiguous decision-making) and all inclusion criteria appear met; no exclusion criteria met from abstract.
Empirical study with original data reporting human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task inside an MRI scanner, matching review scope. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract is an editorial/opinion piece for dietitians with no original human fMRI data or decision-making task described. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (original empirical data), I2 (fMRI during risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making), I3 (human sample performing such a task).

Abstract reports an original fMRI study (English) where human participants performed a sequential risk-taking decision task; results pertain to neural responses during risky decision-making and attentional focus. No exclusion criteria met (not PET/review). Include for full-text review to extract relevant fMRI contrasts and participant details.

Abstract describes an empirical English-language fMRI study examining decision-making and risk-taking behavior in human patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, implying task-based risky decision-making during scanning. This meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are apparent from the abstract.

Abstract reports original human data in English, used fMRI during a probabilistic classification (feedback-driven) decision task, and includes clinical (stroke) and control samples. This meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I3; no exclusion criteria apply. Task appears to involve decision-making under uncertainty relevant to risky/ambiguous decision processes, so include for full-text review to confirm task mapping to review domains.

Abstract reports an empirical human study on methamphetamine-dependent participants and addresses risky decision making with functional connectivity (implying fMRI). However the abstract does not explicitly state that fMRI was conducted while participants performed a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task (I2 not clearly demonstrated). Include for full-text review to confirm task-based fMRI methods.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study using human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task with ambiguous (male vs female) faces, meeting inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I3; no exclusion criteria are met (not a review and uses fMRI).

This is an empirical English fMRI study where human participants performed a risky gambling decision-making task across age groups, meeting I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET-only or review) are met. Include for full-text review.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study in human participants performing perceptual decision-making tasks; no exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) apply. Suitable for inclusion in the meta-analysis and full-text review.

English empirical fMRI study of risky decision-making in human participants (amphetamine/MDMA users and controls). All inclusion criteria (I1-I3) are met; no exclusion criteria apply (not PET or a review).

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study in humans examining choices between certain outcomes and risky gambles, meeting inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (e.g., non-fMRI or review) are met. Include for full-text review to confirm details.

English-language empirical fMRI study with original data in healthy young adults. The task manipulated probabilistic evaluation and risk in pronoun reference resolution, recruiting DLPFC and OFC—fits risky/ambiguous decision-making fMRI studies. Include for full-text review to confirm task details and coordinates.

fMRI study with human participants performing monetary gambles involving prospective effort and risk, meeting criteria for risky decision-making. Study is an empirical original-data article in English; no exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) are met.

Abstract examines decision-making under uncertain conditions in healthy individuals (meets I3). The imaging modality (fMRI) is not specified in the abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone. No exclusions identified. Include for full-text review to confirm fMRI use and other details.

This study validates motor and language fMRI against direct cortical stimulation in a neurosurgical context and does not report fMRI during risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making tasks (I2 not met). No exclusion criteria are met.

Empirical, English-language human study of perceptual decision making with causal TMS and fMRI corroboration. The abstract does not explicitly state that fMRI was conducted while participants performed the task, so inclusion criterion I2 is not clearly satisfied from the abstract alone; full-text review needed to confirm. Include for full-text review.

The abstract describes an English-language empirical study reporting original data collected from human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (random dot motion) with BOLD (fMRI) analyses. This satisfies I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.
Abstract reports an English-language empirical study using fMRI collected during a perceptual decision-making task in humans; meets inclusion criteria and does not meet exclusion criteria.

fMRI study in English reporting original human data during a decision-making task under uncertainty (matching-pennies) with trial-by-trial feedback; meets inclusion criteria I1 (empirical, English), I2 (fMRI during decision-making), and I3 (human participants). Full text can be reviewed for details of task classification (risky vs ambiguous vs perceptual), but abstract provides sufficient evidence for inclusion in full-text screening.

Study reports original English-language empirical data using fMRI while participants played an interactive risky choice game (risky decision-making). Sample includes human participants with OCD and healthy controls. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET-only or review) are met.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study examining neural substrates of risk-taking in adolescents with and without family history of alcoholism — satisfies I1 (original human data), I2 (fMRI during a risk-taking decision task), and I3 (human adolescent sample). Abstract reports original longitudinal human data on neural risk processing and adolescent substance use, but does not explicitly state that functional MRI was used during a decision-making task. Exclusion criteria not met; fMRI status unclear, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Empirical fMRI study (N=29) in English with human participants performing economic decision-making tasks (assurance/coordination and chicken/anti-coordination) in the scanner; these tasks involve risky/ambiguous decision-making. Not a review and not a non-fMRI method.

Abstract describes an empirical human study of neural correlates of risky decision making in anxious youth and healthy controls, but does not explicitly state that fMRI was used during a decision-making task (imaging modality unclear). Include for full-text review to confirm fMRI task procedures.

fMRI study with original human data (probabilistic reversal learning task). However, it is unclear whether the task fits the review’s target categories (risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making). No exclusion criteria met; recommend full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract describes an original English-language human fMRI study of perceptual decision-making (visual motion), reporting empirical data in healthy human participants. This satisfies I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (e.g., non-fMRI methods or review) are met. Include for full-text review.

English-language empirical study reporting original fMRI data collected while human participants performed a perceptual decision-making task (face/house discrimination). This meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I3; no exclusion criteria apply based on the abstract.

Empirical fMRI study in English with original data; human participants performed a reinforcement-learning decision task involving uncertainty (stopping a rotating clock to win points), which fits risky/uncertain decision-making. No exclusion criteria met.

Empirical fMRI study in English with human participants performing a sequential risk-taking task (risky decision-making). This meets I1 (original English empirical data), I2 (fMRI during a risky decision-making task), and I3 (human participants). No exclusion criteria are met from the abstract, so include for full-text review.

Excluded because the study uses verb-generation fMRI to assess language lateralization (presurgical mapping), not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (English empirical study with original data), I3 (human clinical sample—patients with epilepsy). Inclusion criterion not met: I2 (fMRI during risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making). No exclusion criteria met.

Human fMRI study presenting original data on perceptual decision-making (effector-independent accumulation of sensory evidence). Fits the meta-analysis focus on perceptual decision-making; participants are human (healthy). No exclusion criteria met.

Empirical English-language fMRI study in human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (categorization of auditory and tactile stimuli). Meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Empirical fMRI study in humans using a maze navigation task involving decisions under uncertainty (ambiguous/perceptual decision-making). Abstract indicates original data, fMRI during task, and human subjects; no exclusion criteria met (not PET-only or a review).

Event-related fMRI study in English reporting original data on risk-taking decisions in human participants (high- vs low-risk choices). Satisfies I1 and I2. This is an English-language empirical study reporting original data from human participants using fMRI during a spatial-prediction task (a perceptual decision-making paradigm). It satisfies I1, I2, and I3, and no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study in humans performing risky decision-making; neural measures of valuation during choice were collected. No exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) apply. Include for full-text review to extract task and imaging details.

Abstract reports original empirical data in English including two human fMRI studies where participants made choice tasks (olfactory and warm pleasantness choices) examining decision difficulty/confidence, meeting I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET-only or review) are met. Included for full-text review to confirm task fits perceptual decision-making inclusion.

Abstract reports an empirical experiment on the neurobiological influence of expert advice on financial decisions under risk but does not explicitly state that fMRI was used or detail the participant sample. I1 (empirical/original data) is satisfied; I2 (fMRI during task) and I3 (sample explicitly human) are not demonstrated in the abstract. Include for full-text review to confirm fMRI and participant details.

Original empirical fMRI study in English examining tactile spatial pattern discrimination (a perceptual decision-making task) in human participants. Meets I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria (non-fMRI or review) are met.

Study reports original fMRI data in humans (healthy volunteers) and includes a decision-making task (delay discounting), satisfying I1 and I3. Include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Meets inclusion: original empirical fMRI study in humans performing a probabilistic (risky) decision-making task; participants are adolescent girls (human sample). No exclusion criteria met (not PET/review). Abstract provides sufficient detail to include for full-text review.

Study is an English-language empirical fMRI study with human participants (recovered anorexia and controls), satisfying I1 and I3. No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract reports original fMRI data in human younger and older adults performing a state-based decision-making task, but it does not specify that the task involved risk, ambiguity, or perceptual decisions. Insufficient information to confirm I2, so include for full-text review.

Abstract reports an original fMRI study in human adolescents with anxiety addressing neural responses to uncertainty (satisfies I1 and I3). Abstract reports human fMRI data and behavioral effects on risk taking, but it is unclear whether the fMRI was conducted during a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task (the gambling task was a separate experiment and may not have been scanned). Abstract reports original empirical fMRI data collected in human participants during perceptual (and rule-based) decision-making tasks, meeting inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria (non-fMRI methods or review) are met. Full-text review warranted to extract peak coordinates and other details.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study with original human participant data performing decision-making under reducible vs. irreducible uncertainty (addresses risky/ambiguous decision processes). Original empirical study with human OCD patients and matched controls addressing decision-making and prefrontal cortical function, meeting I1 and I3. Abstract reports original empirical human fMRI data (multivoxel BOLD) collected while participants performed a sequential inference task that involves perceptual/uncertainty-driven decision-making. Meets I1, I2, and I3. No exclusion criteria are met from abstract information.

English-language empirical study reporting original fMRI data collected while human participants performed a risky decision-making task (repeated deck choices with stochastic payoffs). Fits the meta-analysis objective; no exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports an original English-language fMRI study of decision-making under risk and ambiguity in human pathological gamblers and controls; meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study with original data (I1). Participants performed a perceptual decision-making task (motion coherence discrimination) during task-fMRI (I2). Abstract reports an original empirical English-language fMRI study in human adolescents performing a risk-taking decision-making task. Abstract indicates an empirical fMRI study of risky decision-making in humans with HIV, implying original data in English and that participants performed risky choice tasks during functional MRI. Abstract reports an empirical human fMRI study (I1) with human participants (I3) but does not specify that participants performed a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task (I2 unclear). Abstract reports an English-language empirical fMRI study with original human data (I1, I3) and simultaneous fMRI acquisition during a probabilistic reversal-learning task—a decision-making task under uncertainty—meeting I2. fulltext_screening_results.reason: This is an fMRI study using the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), a risky decision-making task, with event-related modelling of decision (Inflate vs Cash In) and outcome events and parametric modulation by explosion probability. Group-level, whole-brain random-effects voxelwise analyses were conducted and reported (tables/figures). Thus the study provides task-evoked whole-brain contrasts relevant to risky decision-making in humans (schizophrenia and controls). No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, ROI-only, task>baseline only) apply based on the full text. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This fMRI study involves human participants performing a decision-making task that includes risk (probabilities) and effort, and reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results. However, the neuroimaging contrasts reported focus on Shannon entropy (behavioral inconsistency), subjective value in low-entropy pairs, and secured-effort contrasts (NRNE>NRME). The paper does not present a contrast that matches the meta-analysis’ required risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision contrasts (e.g., risky > safe, high-risk > low-risk, ambiguity > non-ambiguity, or hard > easy). Importantly, the task is a combined effort-and-risk paradigm and much of the reported imaging results center on effort-related and inconsistency-related contrasts; the meta-analysis explicitly excludes effort-based choice studies (E5). Therefore, although I4, I6, I7 and I8 are satisfied (fMRI during risky/effort decisions, whole-brain maps, eligible participant group, and clear reporting), the study is excluded because it violates E5 and does not provide the requisite risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision contrast (I5 not met).

This fMRI study tested human participants performing a risky decision-making gambling task (GIG task) during scanning, manipulating risk via risky vs safe options and quota conditions. The fMRI analyses report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts comparing decision conditions (quota-severity contrast and Low/High > Non/Imp and Non/Imp > Low/High), with activation maps and coordinates and cluster correction. Participants were healthy humans. Thus the study meets inclusion criteria for fMRI risky decision-making, condition-vs-condition contrasts, group whole-brain results, participant eligibility, and availability of results in text/figures. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, only ROI, only connectivity without activation, contrasts vs rest only) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This paper reports task-based fMRI collected while human participants performed a risky decision-making task (CUPS) and includes condition-vs-condition contrasts (risky vs non-risky and parametric modulators of risk and reward). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses were performed and reported (FLAME random-effects, cluster-corrected maps, tables/figures with coordinates). Participants include casual methamphetamine users and non-users, which is acceptable per study population criteria. The study therefore meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7 and I8 and does not violate any exclusion criteria (not PET, not ROI-only, not resting-state/connectivity-only, and not task>baseline only). Full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion; fulltext appears complete.

This is an empirical fMRI study with healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (categorizing average color/shape). The authors report group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise SPM8 analyses (parametric and contrast-based tests of mean-related and variance-related uncertainty) with peak coordinates and cluster-corrected results, satisfying contrasts equivalent to hard>easy / uncertainty contrasts. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not rest-baseline-only contrasts, and task is perceptual DM).

This fMRI study of slot-machine outcomes reports whole-brain, group-level activation maps with coordinates and includes pathological and non-pathological gambler groups (meets I6, I7, I8). However, it does not test risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making contrasts as defined by the review (e.g., risky>safe, high- vs low-risk, ambiguity contrasts). The reported contrasts are outcome-processing contrasts (wins vs losses, large-win vs small-win), not condition contrasts that manipulate decision uncertainty or risk at the time of choice. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E5 (task is not a risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making task per meta-analysis definitions). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (task mapped to risky/ambiguous/perceptual DM) and I5 (required decision-making contrasts). Full text appears complete. Hence EXCLUDED.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision task (face/house discrimination) with concurrent metacognitive (confidence) reports. It includes a within-task condition contrast (Report > Follow) that contrasts an active metacognitive report vs a yoked control, which constitutes a task-versus-control comparison relevant to perceptual decision-making. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects analyses with corrected clusters and tabulated coordinates. Participants and methods are fully described and the full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Thus inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 are satisfied; no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adult humans performing a risky decision-making task (hypothetical treatment choices with explicit side-effect probabilities and efficacies). The authors report within-task contrasts comparing decision conditions (mild > severe and severe > mild side-effect conditions), perform group-level whole-brain voxelwise GLM analyses, and present corrected peak coordinates and figures (FWE-corrected). Methods, results, and discussion are present in the full text. These elements satisfy the review’s requirements for risky decision-making fMRI contrasts and whole-brain group results. No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, ROI-only, task>rest-only contrasts, connectivity-only reporting) are met.

This is an fMRI study of perceptual decision-making (biased vs. unbiased decisions on vocal emotions) in healthy human participants. It reports within-task contrasts directly comparing two decision-making conditions (unbiased > biased and biased > unbiased) and presents group-level voxelwise statistical analyses (SPM flexible factorial, thresholded maps) with ROI-masking applied to whole-brain results. The study therefore provides whole-brain, group-level task-evoked activation maps (reported within predefined ROIs) and also reports functional connectivity (PPI) but not exclusively. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not only baseline contrasts, not only connectivity, not only between-group effects). Full text appears complete with Methods, Results, and Discussion. Hence it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 and should be included in the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study in human participants performing a temporally-extended probabilistic categorization task (perceptual decision-making with uncertainty). The paper reports within-task parametric contrasts (categorical evidence, confidence, and their modulation by urgency — effectively high vs low evidence states) and compares models, with group-level, whole-brain voxelwise statistical maps (SPM analyses, FWER/topological FDR corrections) presented in figures and tables. Participants are healthy adults. The full article contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (not just abstract/metadata). No exclusion criteria (e.g., PET, ROI-only, task>rest-only contrasts, connectivity-only, non-empirical) are met. Therefore the study meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of perceptual decision-making.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants that manipulated ambiguity in a decision-making task (ambiguous, unambiguous, incongruent sequences) and implicitly biased choices. The paper reports within-task condition contrasts including ambiguous > unambiguous and ambiguous > incongruent, and order (2-1 > 1-2) contrasts that directly compare decision-making conditions (matches ambiguous-DM contrast types). Analyses are group-level, whole-brain voxelwise SPM results with FWE cluster correction and reported coordinates/parameter estimates. Participants are healthy adults. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8. No exclusion criteria (E3–E9) are triggered. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an fMRI study in human adolescents performing the Iowa Gambling Task (ambiguous/risky decision-making). It includes condition-versus-condition contrasts relevant to decision-making (advantageous > disadvantageous choices; wins > losses) and reports group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) analyses (with ROI and whole-brain follow-ups). Participant groups (ADHD, OCD, healthy controls) are acceptable under the review’s participant inclusion. Results and coordinates/figures are reported in the text and figures/supplement. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not ROI-only, not task>baseline only). Full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

The study is excluded because it does not meet the requirement that participants performed a decision-making task (Exclusion E5). Although the task manipulates uncertainty (reward vs. no-incentive anticipation) and reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise activation maps, it is a passive slot-machine paradigm with no behavioral choices or decision-making component; thus inclusion criteria I4 (decision-making task) and I5 (at least one decision-making contrast/comparison) are not satisfied. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (whole-brain, group-level voxelwise results reported), I7 (participant group acceptable), and I8 (results clearly described in text/tables/figures). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (fMRI during a risky/ambiguous/perceptual decision-making task), I5 (contrast comparing decision-making conditions or task vs active control for decision-making). Full text is complete and sufficient for this determination.

The study is excluded because its decision task is value-based (pleasantness/reward) rather than a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task as defined by the review (exclusion E5). The paper reports fMRI in humans and contains appropriate contrasts and whole-brain group maps, but the domain of the decision (judging pleasantness of odors / reward-based choice) does not match the meta-analysis target domains. Inclusion criteria met: I5 (within-task contrasts: correct vs error, decision vs rating; ΔI regressors), I6 (group-level whole-brain SPM analyses with coordinates reported), I7 (healthy human participants), I8 (whole-brain results/coordinates reported). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (task is not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task per the meta-analysis scope). No other exclusion criteria applied. Confidence reflects clear domain mismatch based on full text.

This is an fMRI study of risky decision-making using the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) with whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses. The GLM includes condition contrasts (active pumps vs control pumps, parametric modulation by pump number, and pumps following cash-out vs explosion), and results are reported as whole-brain maps and region lists. Core article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Thus it meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for fMRI risky decision-making and provides the necessary whole-brain contrasts and reporting.

Exclusion(s) met: E3. The fMRI analyses reported use task-versus-baseline contrasts (200 ms vs baseline; 400 ms vs baseline) and subsequent regressions/conjunctions derived from those maps; the study does not present a within-task contrast or a task>active-control contrast of the type required. Inclusion(s) met: I4 (fMRI during a perceptual decision-making task), I6 (group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses reported), I7 (healthy human participants), I8 (whole-brain results described in the text/tables/figures). Inclusion(s) not met: I5 (no qualifying decision-making contrast such as hard>easy, low coherence>high, or task>active control; only task>baseline and parametric correlations based on those baseline contrasts). Full text appears complete and not truncated.

Although this fMRI study clearly scanned human participants during a risky decision-making task and reports group-level whole-brain contrasts and coordinates, it does not report any qualified decision-making contrast of the types required by the meta-analysis (e.g., risky > safe, high-risk > low-risk, risk > certainty, ambiguity > non-ambiguity, or perceptual hard > easy). The reported neuroimaging contrasts focus on incidental CS cue processing (Touched_CS > Shocked_CS; Shocked_CS > Touched_CS) prior to gamble presentation rather than contrasts that directly compare decision-making conditions (e.g., risky vs safe choices or task vs control). Therefore inclusion criterion I5 is not met. Inclusion criteria satisfied: I4 (fMRI during risky decision task), I6 (group-level whole-brain analyses reported), I7 (healthy human participants), and I8 (coordinates reported). No exclusion criteria from the provided list apply. Full text appears complete.

This study used fMRI while participants performed the Cambridge Gambling Task (meets I4). It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses with cluster tables and figures (meets I6 and I8) and tested healthy human participants (meets I7). However, the paper’s decision-making contrasts reported for the decision stages are predominantly task>rest contrasts (e.g., color decision vs rest; bet decision vs rest). The only reported condition-vs-condition contrast pertains to outcomes (win vs lose) rather than a decision-making contrast of interest (e.g., risky>safe, high-risk>low-risk, ambiguous>non-ambiguous). Therefore it does not provide an admissible decision-making condition-vs-condition contrast as required by I5. Because the study’s decision-related contrasts are only against rest (implicit baseline), it meets exclusion criterion E3. Conclusion: exclude (fails I5; exclusion E3 applies).

This is an event-related fMRI study in healthy human adults using a risky monetary decision-making task (Wheel of Fortune). It reports within-task contrasts (monetary selection > control selection; high-reward/risk > low-reward/risk) and whole-brain, group-level random-effects voxelwise analyses with tables/figures of coordinates. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets I4 (fMRI risky DM), I5 (task vs control and high-risk>low-risk contrasts), I6 (whole-brain group-level maps), I7 (acceptable participant group), and I8 (results reported in tables/figures/text). No exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete.

This fMRI study used a probabilistic reversal learning task that involves decision making under uncertainty (probabilistic reward contingencies and reversals), matching the review's focus on risky/ambiguous decision-making. fMRI was recorded while participants performed the task (I4). The authors report within-task model-derived contrasts (reward prediction error as a parametric modulator at feedback) and group-level comparisons (including main effects of RPE and OCD>control contrasts), satisfying the requirement for at least one decision-making contrast (I5) and providing whole-brain, group-level voxelwise statistical maps (cluster-corrected) suitable for meta-analysis (I6). Participant groups (patients and healthy controls) are acceptable (I7). Results are reported in-text and in supplementary figures/tables (I8). The study does not violate exclusion criteria: it is not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and includes within-group task effects rather than only between-group contrasts. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical fMRI study in human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (face/house detection). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (random-effects) with statistical contrasts that compare task conditions (e.g., Fin vs Nin; In vs Out; Fin+Hin > Nin), not merely task>baseline. Whole-brain activation maps, figures, and coordinate tables are reported. The task is clearly a perceptual DM paradigm and includes condition-versus-condition contrasts appropriate for inclusion. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for perceptual decision-making fMRI studies and does not meet any exclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis: I4 — BOLD-fMRI was acquired while human participants performed the Iowa Gambling Task (an ambiguous decision-making task); I5 — the primary contrast is decision-making > active non-gambling control condition (decision-making - control); I6 — group-level, whole-brain voxelwise activation maps are reported (normalization, cluster thresholds, group maps described); I7 — participant groups (newly diagnosed T2DM patients and healthy controls) are acceptable per criteria; I8 — whole-brain results are reported in the text, figures and table descriptions. No exclusion criteria apply (not PET, not task>rest-only, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and within-group task effects are reported). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, and data availability).

This fMRI study is excluded because it does not investigate risky, ambiguous, or canonical perceptual decision-making contrasts (Exclusion E5). The task is a sequence/pattern-learning paradigm where subjects identify gradually revealed images to detect patterns; the reported contrasts (pattern vs no-pattern, RT drops, entropy regressors) index structure learning and uncertainty rather than established perceptual difficulty contrasts (e.g., hard>easy, low coherence>high coherence) or risk/ambiguity manipulations. The paper does satisfy several inclusion criteria: I6 (whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses reported using SnPM and cluster-level FWE correction), I7 (healthy human participants), and I8 (whole-brain results clearly described in text/tables/figures). However it does not meet I4 (study must be an fMRI of risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making as defined) nor I5 (contains an admissible decision-making contrast such as perceptual hard>easy or equivalent). Full text appears complete. Therefore EXCLUDED (E5).

This study used fMRI (MID task) but the fMRI task is a reward-processing/anticipation paradigm without an uncertainty or choice manipulation characteristic of risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making tasks. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (whole-brain, group-level voxelwise maps reported), I7 (human participant group acceptable), I8 (whole-brain results described in text). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (fMRI task is not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task), I5 (contrasts are reward-anticipation vs no-reward/loss vs no-loss, which do not match the required risky/ambiguous/perceptual contrasts). Exclusion criteria met: E5 (task is not a risky, ambiguous or perceptual decision-making task; it is reward receipt/anticipation without uncertainty manipulation). Full text appears complete. Therefore study is excluded.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy humans that implements a perceptual decision-making task (face/house discrimination with graded difficulty including noise trials) and reports condition-vs-condition contrasts (e.g., FaceDecision > HouseDecision, parametric contrasts across signal strength/hard>easy manipulations and decision vs instructed responses). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (with cluster correction) including whole-brain reward-network activations; ROI analyses are supplementary but whole-brain results are present in the text/figures. Participants are healthy adults. The full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8 and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy human participants manipulating uncertainty via probabilistic (externally attributed) and knowledge-based (internally attributed) decision tasks. It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (random-effects) with thresholding and provides coordinates/tables and figures. Relevant contrasts include experimental conditions versus an active control task (control blocks with arrows) and parametric contrasts of increasing uncertainty (high uncertainty > low uncertainty), satisfying the meta-analysis contrast requirements. The methods, results, and discussion are present in full. Therefore all inclusion criteria (I4, I5, I6, I7, I8) are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study reports human fMRI during a perceptual decision-making task (delayed match-to-category of auditory and tactile frequency sweeps), with condition-vs-condition analyses (up‑sweep vs down‑sweep) and group-level, whole-brain (surface/voxelwise) statistical maps. Methods describe random-effects GLM univariate contrasts and a surface-based whole-brain searchlight MVPA (SVM) decoding up vs down, with cluster-based correction and conjunctions across modalities. Reporting includes full Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. These elements satisfy the review’s requirements for fMRI perceptual decision-making, a decision-vs-decision contrast, whole-brain group analyses, and acceptable reporting. No exclusion criteria (e.g., task vs baseline only, PET, ROI-only, connectivity-only, or non-empirical) are met. Therefore the article should be included.

This study reports an fMRI experiment (3T scanner) collected while healthy human participants performed a risky gamble decision-making task with explicit probabilities (risky > safe equivalence manipulated across trials). The authors conducted group-level, voxelwise second-level analyses and report condition-vs-condition contrasts (e.g., interactions of decision: gamble vs sure combined with CS effects) rather than task>rest comparisons. Whole-brain results and MNI coordinates are reported (with both an a priori amygdala mask and post-hoc whole-brain exploratory maps). Participants are healthy volunteers. Therefore the paper meets fMRI during risky decision-making (I4), contains decision-condition contrasts (I5), provides group-level whole-brain task-evoked maps (I6) and reports coordinates (I8), and uses an eligible participant group (I7). No exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete for screening.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants that acquired whole-brain, voxelwise group-level task activation maps while participants performed a prediction task based on perceptual sequences. The study includes condition contrasts of interest (structured vs. random sequences; i.e., decision/perceptual task vs. an active control sequence condition), reports whole-brain voxelwise GLM results and corrected statistical maps, and provides coordinates/figures. The task constitutes a perceptual decision-making paradigm under uncertainty (prediction of next stimulus), fitting the review’s perceptual-DM domain. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not task>baseline only, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (intro, methods, results, discussion).

This study reports task-based fMRI during a risky decision-making paradigm (Risky Gains Task) in human participants and includes within-task contrasts (risky vs safe decisions; risky wins vs losses). Analyses are whole-brain, voxelwise group-level results (AFNI preprocessing, voxelwise thresholds, cluster correction via updated 3dFWHMx/3dClustSim) with tables/figures reporting significant clusters and coordinates. Participant sample (occasional stimulant users) is acceptable per the review’s participant inclusivity. The paper provides full Methods, Results and Discussion sections and clearly describes the relevant contrasts, satisfying inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8. No exclusion criteria (E3–E9) are met: contrasts are condition-vs-condition not task>rest, modality is fMRI not PET, the task is a risky-DM task (not excluded task types), whole-brain results are reported (not ROI-only), and the study reports task activation maps rather than only connectivity or resting-state findings. Thus the study should be INCLUDED in the meta-analysis.

This study meets all inclusion criteria for the perceptual decision-making meta-analysis. It used fMRI while human participants performed multiple perceptual decision-making tasks (face–house, happy–angry face, audiovisual synchrony/asynchrony, and random-dot-motion), satisfying I4. The paper reports condition-vs-condition contrasts that map directly onto perceptual-DM comparisons (e.g., difficult > easy; low coherence > high coherence; asynchrony vs synchrony; noisy > clear), satisfying I5. Analyses were performed at the group level using SPM with whole-brain, random-effects second-level maps and corrected thresholds; activations are reported in tables/figures, satisfying I6 and I8. Participants are healthy adults (I7). No exclusion criteria apply: contrasts are condition-vs-condition (not task>rest) so E3 is not met; imaging modality is fMRI (E4 not met); tasks are perceptual DM (E5 not met); whole-brain results are provided (E6 not met); the paper also reports activations beyond connectivity analyses (E7 not met); this is empirical fMRI data (E9 not met). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion, tables). Therefore include.

Although this study used fMRI and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked maps (satisfying I6), recruited healthy human participants (I7), and reports whole-brain results described in the text (I8), it does not meet the review’s decision-making task requirements. The experimental paradigm is a probabilistic learning/inference task probing estimation and confidence about transition probabilities, not a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task as defined by the meta-analysis. It does not present contrasts of the accepted forms (e.g., risky > safe, ambiguous > non-ambiguous, hard > easy) and instead reports parametric/model-based regressors (confidence, surprise, update). Therefore exclusion criterion E5 applies (task is not risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making). Inclusion criteria I4 and I5 are not met.

Exclusion E5 applies: the study's task is intertemporal choice/delay discounting (explicitly listed as excluded in E5). Although the paper used fMRI (I4), reported an ambiguous > exact contrast (I5), provided whole-brain group-level voxelwise maps (I6), included an eligible participant group (I7), and reported whole-brain results in text/tables (I8), the decision-making paradigm is delay discounting/intertemporal choice, which the meta-analysis explicitly excludes. Inclusion criteria met: I4, I5, I6, I7, I8. Inclusion criteria not met: none. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This study is excluded because it does not provide the required whole-brain, group-level voxelwise task activation maps (inclusion criterion I6 not met). Although participants performed perceptual decision-making (random-dot motion) inside an MRI scanner (I4 satisfied) and the paper includes condition contrasts relevant to perceptual DM (e.g., low vs. high coherence; I5 satisfied), the manuscript focuses on behavioral analyses and response-time (LBA) modeling and does not report unmasked, whole-brain fMRI task-evoked statistical maps or voxelwise contrasts. No exclusion criteria from the list (E3–E9) explicitly apply. Summary of criteria: inclusion met = I4, I5; inclusion not met = I6 (whole-brain voxelwise maps absent). Therefore EXCLUDED.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in which human participants performed a sequential risk-taking task (deciding whether to open more boxes with a hidden loss), satisfying the requirement for a risky decision-making task. The paper includes within-task contrasts (e.g., Opt vs Nopt, Nopt vs Devil, GF vs MF) comparing decision-related conditions rather than only task>baseline contrasts. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported with coordinate tables and FWE correction, satisfying the whole-brain evidence requirement; ROI analyses are present but are complemented by whole-brain results. Participants are healthy adults. No exclusion criteria are met (not PET, not only ROI, not resting-state/connectivity-only, not task>baseline only). Therefore all relevant inclusion criteria are met and no exclusions apply.

Excluded because the fMRI data were acquired during a working-memory (n-back) task and not while participants performed a risky, ambiguous, or perceptual decision-making task. Therefore the study does not meet inclusion criteria I4 (fMRI during decision-making task) and I5 (a decision-making contrast/task-versus-control). The study does satisfy I6 (group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked map for the 2-back>0-back WM contrast), I7 (eligible participant groups: patients and healthy controls), and I8 (whole-brain results reported in figures/text). No exclusion criteria (E3–E9) apply. Full text appears complete.

This fMRI study acquired whole-brain, group-level voxelwise activation maps while participants performed a probabilistic classification task (weather prediction task) with uncertainty/predictive-value manipulations and an explicit control task. The methods report whole-brain random-effects analyses and tables of coordinates for task-related activations (presentation and feedback phases) and within-group task activations, satisfying the requirement for task-versus-control and condition-versus-condition contrasts related to uncertainty/predictive value. Participants include stroke patients and controls (eligible participant groups). Results are reported as whole-brain maps and coordinate tables. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria for fMRI of ambiguous/risky/perceptual decision-making and provides whole-brain, group-level results.

The study reports task-based fMRI during a risky decision-making task (Balloon Analogue Risk Task), includes condition-vs-control contrasts (mean pump events vs control-balloon events) and parametric modulation contrasts (risk/reward indexed by pump number), and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise results (cluster-corrected whole-brain analyses). Participant groups (methamphetamine users and healthy controls) are acceptable. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, discussion and limitations, so appears complete. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5, I6, I7, and I8, and violates no exclusion criteria.

This study reports an fMRI experiment with healthy human participants performing a perceptual decision-making task (gender-ambiguous face perception) and compares ambiguous vs. unambiguous conditions, so it meets inclusion criteria I4, I5 and I7. However, the fMRI analysis is performed as ROI-based variance analyses (bilateral SPL and IPL) without reporting a group-level whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked statistical map. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E6 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results) and fails to satisfy inclusion criterion I6 (whole-brain, voxelwise group task map not provided). Full text appears complete. Based on these points, the study is excluded from the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical fMRI study of risky decision-making using a two-choice gambling task (Cake Gambling Task) with human participants. The paper reports within-task condition contrasts (High-Risk > Low-Risk; Gain > No-Gain) and parametric contrasts across reward magnitudes. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are described (SPM5; voxelwise t-tests and ANOVAs reported with MNI coordinates and cluster thresholds), and coordinates/clusters are provided in supplementary tables. Participants are healthy human subjects across a wide age range. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis are satisfied and no exclusion criteria are met.

This is an fMRI study in healthy human participants performing perceptual decision-making tasks (criterion comparison and signal detection) with explicit manipulations of difficulty/uncertainty (easy vs difficult; varying coherence/signal level).
